answer.summary: Build a shared, evolving picture of customer and product problems through firsthand product use, a regularly updated problem list, and structured input from stakeholders. Then bring the whole team into the discussion, clarify the core problems together, and revisit the vision and its supporting rationale.

sections.heading: Understand problems firsthand and keep them visible
sections.content: Start by empathizing with customers and getting a visual understanding of their problems; use research to inform that understanding, while also using the product yourself and articulating what works or does not. At the product-cycle level, research can look ahead to foundational problems a couple of cycles out. Maintain a living “Top 10 things you should know” document for each PM: list known problems, which can be qualitative, quantitative, or technical debt, and revise it quarterly.

sections.heading: Build a shared, cross-functional problem set
sections.content: At the start of strategy work, PMs can ask stakeholders—especially those with relevant context, such as marketing, communications, support, research, and content strategy—to contribute their own 10 problems using the same template and rank them. Bring those perspectives together, then do the work of narrowing and clarifying them into the core problems and a final set of 10. Ebi’s example was input that the average reading age of an American is 11, which prompted consideration of whether text should be replaced with images or video.

sections.heading: Keep the whole team aligned through discussion and written outputs
sections.content: Treat problem clarity and context as work the PM helps the team curate together, rather than simply relaying what engineering or design says. Share the vision and its groundwork with the whole team—not only PMs—and present it more than once so people can ask questions and stress-test it. Write up workshop outputs, including insights, strategy, and big rocks, so the shared understanding has a concrete record.

judgment.explanation: The answer accurately describes a living Top 10 problems document that is revised quarterly, and it explains gathering and ranking stakeholder input to shape a shared problem set. However, it does not clearly cover the reference’s specific practice of bringing product, design, data, and engineering partners together to review, discuss, and prioritize the problems; its discussion of the whole team focuses partly on aligning around and stress-testing the vision.
